head.hi: HOW TO BE A GOOD RADIO ACTOR

div.p: The play in this book has actually been produced on the radio. Possibly you have listened to this one when you tuned in at home. The persons whose voices you heard as you listened, looked just as they did when they left their homes to go to the studio, although they were taking the parts of men and women who lived long ago and who wore costumes very different from the ones we wear today.

The persons whose voices you heard stood close together around the microphone, each one reading from a copy of the play in his hand. Since they could not be seen, they did not act parts as in other plays, but tried to make their voices show how they felt.

When you give these plays you will not need costumes and you will not need scenery, although you can easily arrange a broadcasting studio if you wish. You will not need to memorize your parts; in fact, it will not be like a real radio broadcast if you do so, and, furthermore, you will not want to, since you will each have a copy of the book in your hands. All you will need to do is to remember that you are taking the part of a radio actor, that you are to read your speeches very distinctly, and that by your voice you will make your audience understand how you feel. In this way you will have the fun of living through some of the great moments of history.

head.hi: HOW TO FOLLOW DIRECTIONS IN THE PLAY

div.p: There are some directions in this play which may be new to you, but these are necessary, for you are now in a radio broadcasting studio, talking in front of a microphone. The word (in) means that the character is standing close to the microphone, while (off) indicates that he is farther away, so that his voice sounds faint. When the directions (off, coming in) are given, the person speaking is away from the microphone at first but gradually comes closer. The words (mob) or (crowd noise) you will understand mean the sound of many people talking in the distance.

Both the English and the dialect used help make the characters live, so the speeches have been written in the way in which these men and women would talk. This means that sometimes the character may use what seems to you unusual English. The punctuation helps, too, to make the speeches sound like real conversation; for example, you will find that a dash is often used to show that a character is talking very excitedly.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: We take pleasure in presenting this story of Washington crossing the Delaware. The picture of that famous event is familiar to everyone, but the story of what led up to it, and of its importance in American history is not so well known.

The fall and early winter of the year 1776 saw the fortunes of Washington's army sink very low indeed. Beginning with the defeat on Long Island in late August, Washington and his army had met reverse after reverse. They had been forced to retire in succession from Manhattan to Fort Washington, then across the river to Fort Lee, then from Fort Lee to Hackensack. This succession of defeats and the enforced retirements had disorganized and depleted the army. But even worse than that, it had well-nigh ruined the morale of the civilian population, whose hearty support was absolutely necessary if the war was to be carried on. But now, discouraged and disheartened, the mass of the population gave Washington no help, no encouragement, no cooperation.
This is the situation on the morning of November 22, 1776, as we begin our story. Washington is in his headquarters at Hackensack, New Jersey, when Colonel Joseph Reed, his aide, enters—
Have we no information of the British movements yet?
What's the matter with our intelligence service?
It's completely disrupted, sir; and we can get no help from the civilian population.

I know—they've lost all faith in us, Colonel. Nothing but a victory can bring us again the loyalty and help of our own people! It's discouraging, Colonel, to think that now when we need it more than ever before, we can get no help!
Sir, if we could only turn and strike a quick blow, we might recapture Fort Lee.
Yes—if I only knew what force of the enemy is holding the Fort, and when Lord Howe expects to bring the rest of his army across the Hudson.
And without an intelligence service we can't find out! Of course if General Lee would join me—there wasn't any word from Lee this morning, was there?

Oh, why doesn't he answer? Why doesn't he come? It's been more than a week now since I ordered him to join me at once! Have you heard any rumor about him? Has he left Peekskill yet? Has he crossed the Hudson?
I haven't heard a word. He hasn't even acknowledged the last half dozen orders I've forwarded to him.

That's the most discouraging thing of all! If the second in command won't obey orders, is it any wonder that the rest of the army is out of hand? Oh, well! We can't hope to do anything without Lee's help, so there's nothing for us to do but retreat—
Yes, Colonel, our small force is uselessly exposed here. We can't risk capture—that would be the end of everything!
If Lord Howe crosses the Hudson in force, we'd be trapped between the Hackensack and the Passaic Rivers.
So—we've got to begin our retreat at once.
The troops are ready to move, sir. It shouldn't take us long to get out of danger with our small force.
Yes, yes, that's one advantage of a small army, isn't it, Colonel? At least we can retreat rapidly! I suppose the force we have is even smaller today than it was yesterday?
I'm afraid so, sir. The morning report showed less than five thousand present and fit for duty!
If we only had Lee's seven thousand! But we haven't. You may order the retreat at once, Colonel.
We'll move across the Acquackonack bridge, and thence to Newark.
Yes, sir. I'll write the orders, sir. (rattle of paper)
Colonel John Glover with his Marblehead regiment will cover the retreat as usual.
Knox and his artillery will lead. We mustn't lose our guns—the few we have left.
Retreat—retreat—retreat! Is there nothing else in store for us?
Thank you. (rattle of paper) You may send the orders at once, Colonel.
I suppose it's useless to send another order to Lee.
We can send one—I don't think it will have any effect.
He ought to be informed of where we're going—yes, write him again, tell him we're retreating to Newark—
Retreat again I suppose. New Brunswick—Trenton—across the Delaware into Pennsylvania.
Yes sir, if we have any army left by then.

We have some loyal souls who will stand with us to the end. We may have to retreat to the back country of Pennsylvania; but winter is coming, Lord Howe is not an energetic foe, and he will hardly press us after the snow falls. Then if we can fill up our depleted ranks we'll be ready for him in the spring.
Oh, General, if we could only make one stand against the enemy! Make one bold stroke to put new heart into our discouraged countrymen!
I know—I know, Colonel! If Lee would only obey my orders!
I know—and I can't understand his motives!
Why sir, they're perfectly plain to me—and to the rest of the army.
Certainly—he wants to discredit you—to bring about your failure—so that he can succeed to your command!
So—? (pause) Well, if Lee can bring victory where I have failed, I'll be only too glad to step down in his favor.
Sir, I beg of you, you mustn't even entertain such a thought, why General Lee could no more—(knock)
Will you see who it is, Colonel.
Yes, sir—(mumble at a distance, then out loud) General, there's a man here who wants to see you.
He refuses to give his name, and says his business is private.
Yes, sir—(off) Come on in, the General will see you.
Thankee—thankee, sir. I'm obleeged to ye, sir. (in) Be ye General Washington?
I am, and what can I do for you?
I'd like to see ye alone—sir—it's important!

An' I've had tarnation's own time gittin' here—I cal'ate half yer army stopped me an' wanted to know my name an' my business—an' they wasn't goin' to let me in when I wouldn't tell 'em. But it takes more'n that to stop John Honeyman when he gits sot on doin' something.
That's me, sir, an' I promised Marthy—that's my wife, sir—that I'd come to see ye—and I come, an' here I be!
And what can I do for you, Mr. Honeyman?
I come to make ye an offer.
I'm in a way to find out a lot o' things that's goin' on in the British Army.
Aye, ye see, I'm a butcher.
An' I've got a contract to supply the redcoats with beef. Now they think I'm a good Tory! But General, I ain't!
An' I figgered that mebbe I could find out things an' tell ye about 'em—if we could fix things up.
How much do you want for your information?
No! No! General! I ain't tryin' to sell ye nothin'!
I beg your pardon, Mr. Honeyman. But I have so many insincere offers.

I know—I know! I hear folks talk. They think I'm a Tory! Wal', sir, I want they should keep on a-thinkin' it! I cal'ate if I'm a-goin' to be any use to ye, nobody must know I ain't a rip-roarin' all-fired Tory.
An' that's the why I wouldn't tell none o' yer men what my name er my business was.
Mr. Honeyman, you've shown extraordinary good sense! You're exactly the man I've been looking for! I'm in desperate need of reliable information. And I believe you're the man to get it for me.
Lord Cornwallis is bringin' 15,000 men across the Hudson tonight, to git ye.
That's fu'st-rate! Now I'll be goin'—an' I'll keep ye informed when I know anything ye ought to know.
Just a moment, Honeyman. How are you going to get your information to me?
Wal', I figger I might come to see ye—
No, you'd be sure to excite suspicion.
I'd be as keerful as could be.
No—I mustn't even let my own men know you're working for me.

Wal'—ye might have me captured now an' agin—tell yer men I'm a notorious Tory—an' have 'em be on the lookout fer me particular! Then when I've got something fer ye, I'll put myself in the way o' gittin' captured.
Good! That's an excellent idea. I'll have to give you a pretty bad name with my troops.
And I don't know how I can reward you.
I don't need no reward to help ye, General Washington, I got a duty to do that!—There's only jest one thing, sir—
I'd sorta—er—kinda like my wife an' children protected from the—wal'—the results o' my bein' an active an' notorious Tory.
Ye see, I don't mind what folks think o' me, but Marthy—that's my wife, sir—she an' the young un's might git—wal'—treated pretty shabby.
I understand. I'll give you an order for them to use in case of necessity.

Certainly! Here—I'll write it now. (rattle of paper) Let's see—(slowly) "To the Good People of New Jersey and all others it may concern: It is ordered that the wife and children of John Honeyman of—" Where's your home?

"—of Grigstown, the notorious Tory now within the British lines and probably acting the part of a British spy, should be protected from all harm and annoyances. This is no protection to Honeyman himself." Is that satisfactory?
I cal'ate that covers it, sir.
Very well, I'll sign it—(signing) There you are, sir.
I'm much obleeged to ye, sir.
No, Honeyman, I'm the one who is your debtor. Good day, sir.
Good day, General Washington. Next time ye see me I'll be yer prisoner.

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: And John Honeyman left Washington's camp to set about making his position secure with the British. He became one of the regular meat contractors for Cornwallis's army, which pursued Washington across the state of New Jersey during the next month.

Washington did not hurry his retreat, but he always got away. Finally about the first of December, he came to Trenton, where he halted for a week and sent men up and down the river to collect all the boats on the Delaware. He knew that he would be forced to retreat into Pennsylvania; and he proposed to leave no means for the enemy to follow him. On December 8, 1776, the British advance, which consisted of a brigade of Hessians under Colonel Rall, entered Trenton; but as usual, Washington was half a day ahead of his pursuers, and as the Hessians entered the village, the rear guard of the Americans was just entering the last of the boats, and safely pulled away to the Pennsylvania shore! Lord Howe, who had joined Cornwallis, sent out men to look for boats, but none could be found. The weather turned cold. Lord Howe was uncomfortable; so he decided to put his troops into winter quarters and let the pursuit go. He had done enough for one season!
He and Cornwallis arranged to scatter the troops about New Jersey to hold that territory, while they went back to New York to enjoy the winter.

Trenton was left in charge of Colonel Rall and his brigade of Hessians. On December 22, John Honeyman drove a small herd of cattle into Trenton, left them standing in front of headquarters, as he went up and knocked on the door. (knocks)
Aye, it's me—an' I got some cattle out front here fer yer Quartermaster.
Well, that's good news—my men will be glad to see that beef! Now we can give 'em a Christmas dinner that'll be a Christmas dinner!
All ye need now, Colonel, is a mite o' wine, eh?
Never fear, we've got the wine!
Wal', ye kin have a fu'st-rate Christmas then.
Yes sir! With roast beef and two hogsheads of fine wine—we should do very well.
Two hogsheads won't go so far with a whole brigade.
Oh, I haven't got a whole brigade.
No, just a thousand men, that's all! Why sir, they can all get roarin' drunk on the ration I'll issue 'em.
An' like as not they will, eh, Colonel?
Well, Honeyman, what do you expect o' soldiers? Christmas you know—and out here in this God-forsaken place. Let 'em get drunk, I say. There's nothing else to do.
Wal', Colonel, I cal'ate 'tain't often ye find a better officer than ye be! I'd like to serve under ye!

Yes, sir. I'd do it if I wasn't helpin' along things in my way by roundin' up food fer the king's men. Wal', mebbe ye better sign fer these critters out in front an' I'll be gittin' along. I got to hike over to the next post. Er—by the way—how fer is it to the next detachment o' troops?
Six miles, huh? How fer to the next one north?
No, I'm command of the flank. This is the last post.
I cal'ate that makes a lot o' hard work fer ye, Colonel?
Sure, don't ye have to patrol up an' down the river, an' sich like things?
Wal', after all, there's some o' the enemy left, ain't there?
A half-a-dozen starved ragamuffins. What could they do to my trained Hessians?
Not much, I cal'ate! Ye ain't in much danger, an' that's a fact!
If we had some boats we'd soon make short work of them. But confound the rascals, they made away with all the boats.
Ye ain't got no boats, eh?
Wal'—if ye want to git across the river—
Oh, we'll get across as soon as the river freezes over. We'll get the last o' the rebels then.
Wal', Colonel, good luck to ye. But I hope ye won't be in too big a hurry to capture all the rebels!
Er—I'll be out of a job; and so'll ye be, Colonel!
Yes, that's right too. Well, let's have a look at your cattle and I'll sign for 'em.
Thanks—hm—how many did you say there were?
There's twenty-two critters there—er, there was when I drove 'em up.
Two—four—five—seven—ten (etc.) Hm—twenty-one's all I make, Honeyman.
Twenty-one? Pshaw now—did one o' them critters go trapsin' off. (he counts) Yes sir, that's just what's happened. Wall—sign fer the twenty-one, an' I'll go out lookin' fer that other critter.
Here you are—let me have that bill—(rattle of paper) Twenty-one in good condition, signed—Rall. There you are. Hope you find the other one.
Thankee—where's that road off to the left go?
I cal'ate the critter musta gone that way.
Better keep a sharp lookout if you go down that way.
Some o' those ragamuffin rebels might be on this side of the river.
Pshaw now—ye don't say! They come across the river, do they?
Yes, once in a while. But they don't dare bother us. But they might pick up a civilian.

lg.l: Oh, I cal'ate I kin take keer o' myself. I got my whip and this halter.
That ought to be enough to scare 'em away from you!

div.p: They'll figger I'm the hangman come out to git 'em—fetchin' my halter along! (he and RALL laugh)

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: So Honeyman started down the river road, cracking his whip and swinging his halter. A couple of miles down the road, four Continental soldiers were in hiding. They had been sent out with instructions to pick up a prisoner, if possible, and bring him into Washington's headquarters for the purpose of securing information. As Honeyman drew near their place of hiding in the brush alongside the river road, the men heard the snapping of his whip. (crack of whip)
Don't know, sounds funny. See anything, Corporal?
There, I see him! Huh, it's just a farmer crackin' his driving whip.
Yah, I see him. What's he got in his other hand?
Looks like a piece o' rope.
Yep. A halter. Well, no use stoppin' him. Lie low. We want to get one o' them Hessians. By George, though, I'd like to have that whip.
To use on the Hessians we're goin' to git!
You bet. Them mercenaries ought to be whipped out o' the country! Shootin's too good for 'em—we'd ought to—
Yah? What about it? Keep quiet, I said!
No! Listen, Corporal, we got to capture him.
The General issued orders about him.
That's who it is. Let's grab him.
Men! (several voices respond) We're going to take this fellow. All right now—lie low—and when I give the signal, jump!
So-o-o, boss—where's that dang critter gone to? I cal'ate mebbe—
Say! What's the matter—what ye doin'!
Come on! Grab him! Get hold of him there! Down with him! (etc.)
Hey, you scoundrels! Git off me! Leave me be! I'm a peaceable man, ye ain't got no right to do this to me—git off me—git off—I say—hey, leave go my halter!
Well, ain't this nice, boys. He's brought along a rope for us to tie him up with, now ain't that thoughtful—here—leave go the rope.
Let me up—don't ye tie me up! I'm jest a farmer—out huntin' a stray cow!
Stray cow, eh? Well, we was huntin' a stray coward! (laughter) Here give me that whip!
Here ye are, Corporal! Well boys, take a look at him—this here's Honeyman the Tory. (all comment)
All right, throw him into the boat! General Washington'll be right pleased to see ye, Mister Honeyman! Come along—oh, ye won't go, eh—well, fetch him, boys.
Leave me be! Stop it! The King's men'll make ye pay fer this.
Hey shut up—grab him Tom—stop that kickin', fetch him along. (etc.)

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: Protesting and struggling, Honeyman was thrown into the boat and carried to the Pennsylvania shore of the Delaware. In the meantime, on that very afternoon of December 22, 1776, Washington was holding a council of war with his staff.
Gentlemen, I regret to inform you that Congress has fled from Philadelphia.
What? Fled? Left Philadelphia? Too bad! (etc.)
I'm sorry! I asked them particularly to stay there, as I feared the effect on the people of the country. But it seems that even Congress has lost faith in the army.
We've got to do something to re-establish their faith! (all agree)
Yes! But what? Charles Lee is captured—his army gone—we can't look for any help from that quarter.
Sir, can't we go back across the river, suddenly—and strike a blow before the enemy knows what we are up to?

We'll have to! It's our only hope. But how, when, and where? I had hoped that we might get information that would guide us in our plans. Well, we haven't got it! Now, much as I hate to make any move without full and complete information, I don't see what else we can do. The river will be frozen over in a week or ten days. That means that the enemy can cross over and chase us whither they please! If we are to do anything, we've got to do it now! I've called you here to lay this before you. Will you follow me on a blind chance?
Yes! We will! You can count on us, sir. (etc.)

I want you all to realize that this is a desperate chance. Failure means—well, we might as well face it—it means the end of our cause; but success—well, gentlemen, we can only hope and pray for success! (knock) Will you see who's at the door, Colonel Reed?
Tell whoever it is to come back later—I'm in council.
Yes, sir. (a mumble at the door) I beg pardon, sir, they've just brought in a prisoner.
Good, tell them to wait outside.
They say, sir, it's Honeyman the Tory, and you left orders—
Honeyman? Excellent! Gentlemen, I must ask you to leave me.
You may hold yourselves in readiness for action. I'll issue the orders shortly.
Bring the prisoner in, Colonel Reed.

lg.l: Yes, sir. Bring him in, men.

div.p: Here he is, General, that Tory you wanted, sir.
Very good, men. You may go.
Can you handle him safe, sir?
He seems to be well bound. I think I'll have no trouble.

lg.l: Yes, sir. Very good, sir. Come on, men. We'll wait outside, sir.
Well, Honeyman. We've got you at last, eh?

div.p: I demand to be set free. Ye'll all answer to yer King fer this. (door shuts)
Across the river in Trenton there ain't but a thousand Hessians.
Colonel Rall, and he ain't none too keerful—no patrols up er down the river—nobody at all north of him, and six miles to the nearest post on the south of him.
Excellent—excellent! We can do it! I'll order the attack tomorrow night! We'll trap them! We'll fight for once instead of retreat—we'll—
If yer figgerin' on attackin', the time is Christmas night!
On Christmas the Hessians are goin' to git a big issue o' heavy wine, an' wal'—General—ye know soldiers—I don't have to say no more!
Good! Christmas night! Yes that's it! Has Colonel Rall taken any precautions against surprise?
Nary a one that I could see. He ain't a mite o' use fer you er yer soldiers. Ragamuffins he called 'em.
Ragamuffins? Yes, they are, poor fellows, but Honeyman, we'll see—perhaps ragamuffins can fight when they're given the chance—and with this information, you have given us our chance!
Wal', sir, I thought ye'd like to know.
Now, shall I turn you lose, Honeyman?
No, General, I figger ye'd better treat me like a prisoner er I can't be any more use to ye.
True, very well then. I'll have you put in the guardhouse and contrive to have you escape.
Tell the Corporal who's waiting out there to come in and take his prisoner to the guardhouse.
Yes, sir—Corporal, come take charge of your prisoner.
Come on, men! Fall in around the prisoner—and look sharp that he doesn't try anything—forward march! (sound of feet receding)
Christmas night! Trenton—God be with us!

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: That night, by some unexplained accident, John Honeyman escaped from the guardhouse and returned to the British lines, where he continued his valuable service for the American cause.
Washington, with the information that Honeyman had brought him, was able to lay his plans intelligently and carefully.

Just after dusk has fallen on Christmas night, Washington orders his troops to the shore of the river. Snow is falling and the wind is howling, as Washington and Knox stand together near the boat landing—(wind and murmur of crowd with occasional sharp commands in background through this scene.)
This weather ought to help us, Knox.
Brrr—it's cold enough to keep the Hessians indoors—if that's what you mean, General.
The snow will cover our movements.
Yes—in more ways than one, General.
Very good. (lower) Order embarkation to begin, Knox.
No, a company of foot soldiers first to stand guard and protect the landing.
Send one of your companies across first to stand guard and protect the landing.
Very good, sir. Company A, into the boats! (orders and mob confusion)
The river looks bad, sir. See all the ice? It looks wicked!
The boatmen say they can't make it, sir.
Can't make it? But they've got to!
Sorry sir, they say the floating ice—
Glover! Colonel Glover! Pass the word for Colonel Glover. (order repeated several times at different distances)
We've got to get across, Knox, we've got to! If this attempt fails, there's nothing left for us! Nothing!
We'll get across, sir, if we have to swim.
Colonel Glover, can your regiment of seafaring men handle our boats in that river?
General Washington, my men can handle boats in any water!
The boatmen say they can't cross because of the floating ice.
Sir, my men are sea sailors, not river boatmen—it takes more than ice to scare them off!
Good! Put some of them in every boat.
And you will take general charge of the entire fleet.
Tell them to listen to General Knox's commands. He is the only one whose voice can be heard in this storm!
Very good, sir! (going out) This way, the Marblehead regiment! This way to the boats! (mob)

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: For the next nine hours the difficult work of crossing the ice-filled river went forward. Colonel Glover and his regiment of seafaring men from Marblehead, Massachusetts, performed almost miraculous service in landing every man, horse, and gun without losing anything!
It was five o'clock in the morning of December 26 when Washington, now on the Jersey shore of the river, turned to Knox—(wind and crowd noise)
Has the last boatload landed, Knox?
Company—company! (etc.) Attention! First regiment is formed, sir, second—(etc.)
Men, we are about to start upon our most important offensive. Upon the results of our efforts this morning depends the outcome of our struggle for liberty and independence.

I shall take the first brigade and half the artillery with me down the Pennington road. The rest of the detachment under command of General Green will take the river road. It should take us about four hours to reach the outposts of Trenton. Now, it is necessary for us to attack simultaneously, so will the officers all set their watches with mine. It is now just five o'clock and ten minutes. At nine o'clock, attack!
Let every man march quietly, keep in good order in the ranks, give prompt obedience to his officers, and bear in mind the watchword—Victory or Death! March your men off!

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: Thus, on that cold and stormy December morning, the half frozen, desperate band of ragamuffin soldiers started its march toward Trenton—toward its last forlorn hope. Washington prayed that he might catch the garrison of Hessians unsuspecting and unprepared; but he feared that he had taken so long to effect the crossing of the ice-filled river that he could not surprise the enemy!
As a matter of fact, warning was sent to Colonel Rall, but that officer, secure in his belief that no effective force of Colonial soldiers could be sent against him, paid no attention to the warning.
It was nearly nine o'clock when the Corporal of the advance guard of Washington's detachment hurried back to report to the General.
General Washington, we've sighted the enemy outpost.
It lacks five minutes of the time set! Oh, Corporal—
Did you see any sign of General Green's command on the river road?
We saw 'em a half hour ago, sir, as we came over that hill back there.
Yes, sir, a little ahead of us, sir.
This storm has likely ruined the flintlocks.
No doubt of that, sir—we'll have to use bayonets.
Order bayonets fixed, and the troops deployed ready to charge bayonets on command.
Brigade, fix bayonets! (voices repeat order, etc.) Shall the artillery lead or follow, sir?
Follow and take position at the head of every street.
Deploy your troops—prepare to charge bayonets! (command repeated—mob noise as order is obeyed)
Keep your ears open for firing—it's nearly time. (musketry)
Green has started! Order the charge, Knox! And God be with us!
Forward! Charge bayonets! Ho! (a great roar from the mob as the charge begins)

div.head: ANNOUNCER
div.p: So Washington and his men swept into the village of Trenton, catching the Hessians totally unprepared! In an hour and a half it was all over. The disposed army of ragamuffins put the Hessians to rout! It was the first great American victory of the Revolution, and its effect was enormous. The discouraged Colonists suddenly received new heart. Hope for the cause of independence had a rebirth, and Washington, instead of fighting a losing battle alone, found himself the leader of his countrymen in fact, as well as in name! In crossing the Delaware, Washington had saved the cause of American independence!

div.head: Transcriber's Notes
div.p: Page 8: Changed You're to Your. (You're name is John Honeyman?)
